items.title: Frank Turek Fights ‘War on Reality,’ Offers Warning for America
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "Dystopia"
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Apologist Frank Turek is on a mission to tackle the “war on reality,” warning Americans face a “dystopia” if the nation continues marching toward Marxism.

Turek’s new book, “The War on Reality Workbook: Recovering Truth in a World That Celebrates Lies,” is being released as the nation recently remembered the one-year anniversary of the assassination of conservative and Christian commentator Charlie Kirk.

The apologist told CBN News he and his coauthor, Phoenix Hayes, dedicated the book to Kirk, calling the late Turning Point USA founder a “warrior for reality.”

Turek broke down the current state of culture and decried many elements that simply make no logical — or biblical — sense.

“Abortion is healthcare; we’re pulling baby body parts out of women, and we’re calling that health care,” he said. “That’s a war on reality, and Charlie was a casualty in the war on reality. But, thankfully, since he was a believer, all the murderer was able to do is change his address.”

Turek continued, “He’s absent from the body, present with the Lord, and we remain behind, still engaged in fighting for reality when so many forces are fighting against.”

items.title: Christian Singer Colton Dixon Says Charlie Kirk’s Assassination ‘Changed’ Him
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: "It gave me a new outlook on things."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Christian singer-songwriter Colton Dixon said the assassination of Charlie Kirk and the government’s restrictive response to the COVID-19 pandemic “changed” him.

Dixon, 35, told CBN News seeing Kirk murdered for exercising his right to free speech pushed him “to seek truth harder.”

“I feel like, just for a lot of people, whether you believed in what Charlie stood for or not, just for a lot of people, it was, like, it just — I don’t know, it changed me,” said Dixon. “It was just, like, ‘Wow.’ [It] gave me a new outlook on things, even just to seek truth harder.”

The up-and-coming generation, he added, aren’t taking things at face-value anymore, regardless of the source. “They’re seeking truth for themselves,” he explained.

As a Christian recording artist, Dixon said he believes he has found the answer: “The answer’s Jesus.”

The recent spate of culture-defining events have, according to the “Build a Boat” singer, “anchored my feet down in my beliefs so that I’m not going to be pushed around by a little Chihuahua who might bark louder.”

“I kind of even really figured out why I believe what I believe,” he said. “[B]ecause again, it’s just COVID and just all these different things, they’re trying to get you to do different things and I’m like, ‘OK, why aren’t we just going to do it?’ Let’s figure out why so we’re not just being stubborn [and] hardheaded.”

“We open up God’s Word, we pray, we seek godly wisdom, and then we come to the conclusion, ‘Oh, this is why,'” Dixon said. “So now I just feel more steadfast in why I believe what I believe.”

As he’s ruminated on his convictions in recent years, Dixon has become noticeably more comfortable creating edgier content — at least edgier for the status quo in the contemporary Christian music world.

The “American Idol” alumnus just released a new song, “Bones,” based on the Old Testament passage of Ezekiel 37, chronicling the story of the prophet being transported to a valley filled with dry bones. God asked whether the bones could live and then commanded Ezekiel to prophesy over them. As the prophet began speaking promises to the bones, they assembled and were covered in flesh. Then a second prophecy called breath to fill their lungs and they became a living army standing to their feet.

Dixon said the song is “straight from Scripture,” recalling reading the biblical account and feeling “super inspired” and “like God gave me revelation” about speaking “over the dead things in your life.”

During a time of year when most of American culture is fixated on death from a secular perspective, Dixon saw an opportunity to flip the script around Halloween with a biblical understanding of death.

“What if we could … take this passage that already theatrically lines up with a lot of the visuals of skeletons — that’s what this whole passage was, it was a valley of dry bones, the bones rattling, coming together, flesh coming upon the bones, it was like zombies out there, you know, in Ezekiel 37,” he reflected.

That passage of Scripture, Dixon emphasized, shows a biblical interpretation of death, which, for the Christian, he said, is “just a little blip on the timeline of what our lives look like.”

He said, “For the rest of the world, death is the final word. … That’s the period. Life after death is this big mystery. But for a believer, death is not the final word; the cross —what Jesus did on the cross — is the final word, and not only that, but three days later, Him resurrecting from the grave so that we could spend eternal life with Him in heaven. … Death can be a scary thing to talk about, but as a believer, I don’t think it should be.”

The song — and its music video, which is set at night in a graveyard — is certainly unorthodox in its approach, but it paints a clear picture to the world that this life is not all there is. It also tells the story of spiritual power, a nod toward Romans 8:11, where Paul wrote, “The Spirit of God, who raised Jesus from the dead, lives in you. And just as God raised Christ Jesus from the dead, he will give life to your mortal bodies by this same Spirit living within you” (NLT).

“I think that this song is … a kick in the pants for sideline Christians, where I’ve found myself before,” said Dixon. “It’s time to start using the spiritual authority that we have as believers and not just talk the talk, but walk it, as well.”

In fact, for Dixon, it was his wife Annie’s certainty about spiritual authority that led him to do some self-reflection.

“I found myself being so in awe of [my wife] that that was her first response [to pray and speak over things],” he said. “But then also going, ‘Why isn’t that mine?’ You know? If I’m really going to be the best spiritual leader of our house, I need to stop kicking my feet up and actually get in the game and start doing this for real.”

items.title: The Most-Searched Thing in the Bible App This Year Was Psalm 91. ‘Anxiety,’ ‘Hope’ and ‘Healing’ Weren’t Far Behind.
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: The search bar in a Bible app works like any other, which means it shows what people are worried about before they’ve said it out loud to anyone. YouVersion says “Psalm 91” was the single most-searched term in the app this year. In its newest release, the company also says “anxiety,” “hope” and “hea
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

The search bar in a Bible app works like any other, which means it shows what people are worried about before they’ve said it out loud to anyone.

YouVersion says “Psalm 91” was the single most-searched term in the app this year. In its newest release, the company also says “anxiety,” “hope” and “healing” were among the year’s most searched terms. YouVersion describes Psalm 91 as a psalm that encourages readers to turn to God for refuge and comfort in difficult times. The psalm runs 16 verses. Together, YouVersion says, the searches offer a glimpse into the personal questions and hopes people are bringing to Scripture.

Daily use of the Bible App grew by more than 13% compared with 2025, reaching 18.5 million people a day. It also says it added more than 160 million new installs across its family of apps in 2026, after celebrating one billion installs last November. Daily engagement grew faster than installs, which the company reads as a sign that people are returning to the app and not only downloading it.

Some of the highest engagement is outside the U.S. YouVersion says it sees some of the highest levels of Bible App engagement in Sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East and Southeast Asia, and it is building regional hubs in places including the United Kingdom, Brazil, Kenya and Mexico. Its apps offer 3,800 versions of the Bible in 2,400 languages, and it works with a network of more than 45,000 churches and partners.

Bobby Gruenewald, YouVersion’s founder and CEO, said in the release that the company has been encouraged by “how many people are turning to Scripture for answers to their questions.”

items.title: What ‘The Conjuring’ Taught Me About the Struggle for Holiness
items.author: Carly Kashmanian
items.summary:
Carly Kashmanian

When we find ourselves in a state of misery or despair, all it takes is a glimmer of light to break through and shift our perspective heavenward.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Carly Kashmanian

I don’t usually stand over a sink of dirty dishes contemplating horror movies (though maybe some do), but that’s exactly what happened recently after a particularly chaotic week of illness and botched morning routines. 

Specifically, I was thinking about a scene from the first Conjuring film (2013), which my husband and I recently rewatched with his teen sister, who had never seen it before. I am not typically a fan of the horror movie genre, but back in my intern days as a young journalist, I was tasked with reviewing the first and second Conjuring films. Something I like about the first film in particular is how it portrays the power of love in conquering evil. 

For those unfamiliar with the plot, Carolyn, a mother of five, becomes possessed by a demonic spirit that had been haunting the Rhode Island farmhouse she and her family recently purchased. Her lack of faith makes her an easy target. By the end of the film, the spirit—a witch named Bathsheba who killed herself on the property after sacrificing her child to Satan (again, not the kind of subject matter I usually find appealing)—has taken full possession of Carolyn, and she is chasing her youngest daughter through the house, attempting to kill her with a pair of shears. It is during this critical moment that medium Lorraine Warren encourages her to fight from the inside. Warren reminds her of a photo hanging in the house that Carolyn had previously shown her: a family beach day she described as one of her most precious memories.

“Carolyn! You have to fight her! Remember what you told me—remember your day at the beach!”

The maternal love evoked by this core memory gives Carolyn the strength to resist the evil entity. With this internal pushback, the exorcism is brought to its completion, and Bathsheba is condemned back to hell. While the Catholicity of the film is dubious (you’d hardly expect James Wan, director of the Saw and Insidious franchises, to be an expert on the Roman rite of exorcism), there is wisdom in this powerful scene: When we find ourselves in a state of misery, despair, or exhaustion, all it takes is a glimmer of light to break through and shift our perspective heavenward to gaze up at Love himself and remember who we are as image-bearers made to love. 

Back to my sink full of dishes. I desire to be a good, holy mother, and I regularly read and pray about what such a life demands. But I so often find myself feeling discouraged and disappointed by my failings. Any parent knows that a single day can bear witness to a range of emotions and events, ups and downs. Throw in illness, sleep deprivation, and perhaps some children with neurodivergence or special needs, and it can feel like a downright assault on the senses. We can begin to forget who we are and how we ended up here. Saints? Us? How?

The real-life American horror story of the Lindsay Clancy murder trial and the months-long social media firestorm it sparked have revealed the hearts of many American women. From the unabashed empathy of many TikTok moms to the shock and disgust at what Anne Hendershott aptly described as a “moral contagion,” the murders of three innocent children have had a polarizing effect akin to the Charlie Kirk assassination just over a year ago. Both of these events point to a modern identity crisis in which people are genuinely divided over basic moral truths. We have become a nation of sick people perpetually on the brink of losing our souls, primed for intellectual and spiritual possession.

The problem of evil is not a new one, and as recent headlines remind us, it certainly isn’t merely the stuff of horror flicks. Perhaps the most unsettling truth, however, is that the internal struggle for peace and order is in fact a normal aspect of the human condition. Novelist and historian Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn famously described the line of good and evil that “passes not through states, nor between classes, nor between political parties either—but right through every human heart—and through all human hearts.”

“This line shifts,” he continues. “Inside us, it oscillates with the years. And even within hearts overwhelmed by evil, one small bridgehead of good is retained.”

The struggle for holiness is not, then, a problem in itself, so long as we persevere. Scripture assures us that even those farthest from God can indeed at any moment become saints. In Luke 15 alone, we find the parable of the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the prodigal son, all of which point to God’s unending mercy. With this blessed assurance, we are instructed on how to proceed:

Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us also lay aside every weight and the sin that clings so closely, and let us run with perseverance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus the pioneer and perfecter of our faith, who for the sake of the joy that was set before him endured the cross, disregarding its shame, and has taken his seat at the right hand of the throne of God. Consider him who endured such hostility against himself from sinners, so that you may not grow weary or lose heart (Heb 12:1-3). 

Study the lives of the saints and you will see countless ways in which ordinary humans have found glimmers of light and grace while burdened and battered by the storms of life. Think of the inextinguishable hope of St. Mother Teresa caring for the sick and wounded “untouchables” of Calcutta with a serene smile on her face. Another beautiful example is St. Gianna Molla, a mother and pediatrician who made the ultimate sacrifice, delaying treatment of an aggressive cancer so her unborn child could live. “The secret of happiness is to live moment by moment and to thank God for all that he, in his goodness, sends to us day after day,” she said.

Those are just two of my favorites. Find yours, befriend them, and ask them to intercede for you.

As we prepare for Hallowtide, let us reflect on what it means to be a saint in our modern world. When we see evil within ourselves, we shouldn’t despair or be surprised. None of us are doomed to become murderers, adulterers, or tyrants. Instead, we should do what Scripture prescribes: look to the saints, fix your eyes on Christ, and remain in him. Remember his promises. We are his. Let us not relinquish our destiny.

items.title: Should Catholics Reclaim Halloween?
items.author: Madeleine Dobrowski
items.summary:
Madeleine Dobrowski

We also ought not give up the fight. Catholics can and should reclaim Halloween, just not in the way that some think.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Madeleine Dobrowski

It’s that time of year again. The leaves rattle crisply down the sidewalks. The evening skies burn orange and pink. Everywhere you look, pumpkins, goblins, witches, and ghouls stand guard on the neighbors’ doorsteps. 

There is no denying it. Over the past couple of decades or so, our culture has seen a significant rise in the popularity of Halloween. What used to be a minor one-day event on the calendar has been transformed into a major seasonal holiday for many families. Terms like “sweater weather” and “harvest” are out. “Spooky season” is in.

Interestingly, it is not just the secular world that has fallen in love with Halloween. It is the Catholic world too. The idea of reclaiming Halloween is trending right now among many Catholics. One simply has to open Instagram in October to be hit with a slew of educational videos from Catholic influencers and major companies, all championing the idea of celebrating Halloween. Not only is it okay, they say. It is good. Not only should Catholics get comfortable with the idea of Halloween. They should embrace it. 

On the other side of the argument are the Catholics who still fear, deep down, that there is something problematic about embracing Halloween. A holiday that seems to glorify death and despair seems at odds with the Christian message of hope and the dignity of human life. 

Who is right? Is it even possible for Catholics to reclaim Halloween? In order to answer this question, we must look carefully at the logic on both sides of the argument. 

Those in favor of reclaiming Halloween will almost always point to the same set of facts, which make up what may be called the “historical argument” for celebrating Halloween. This argument explains that Halloween is actually a part of the Catholic liturgical calendar. It constitutes the first night of Hallowtide, a three-night “triduum” of sorts, celebrating the many parts of the Body of Christ. Halloween (originally called “All Hallows’ Eve”) was traditionally the night when Catholics prayed and prepared for the coming feasts of All Saints’ Day and All Souls’ Day. In medieval Ireland and Great Britain, peasants would go door-to-door selling soul cakes in exchange for prayers for the dead. The practice of souling is one of the many traditions that influenced modern-day trick-or-treating. 

Proponents of the historical argument say that because Halloween is Catholic in its roots, we should reclaim the holiday today by celebrating it fully. Trick-or-treating, dressing up, and exchanging candy are harmless nods to these older traditions, much like putting up a Christmas tree in December. Spooky decorations don’t have to be seen as evil, they say. They are a reminder to keep always before us the reality of our own mortality (memento mori), so that we might live not for this earth but for heaven. 

Against the historical argument for celebrating Halloween stands what may be called the “argument from modernity.” This argument focuses not on what Halloween used to be, but on what it has become. The argument from modernity objects that while Halloween may have been celebrated by Christians in the past, it has become a completely secular holiday filled with grotesque and even demonic imagery and practices. 

Proponents of this view are quick to remind us that Halloween stands as the highest feast day on the Satanic calendar. They assert that it is the night of the year on which the most human sacrifice takes place. Ex-witches admit to cursing their property on Halloween night as well as the candy they hand out to unsuspecting children. Proponents of this argument are quick to cite the many ex-occultists and ex-Satanists who emphatically warn Christians against participating in even the most seemingly innocent aspects of Halloween. There is no middle ground when it comes to Halloween, they say. 

Unfortunately, there are problems with both the historical argument and the argument from modernity. The historical argument fails because it equivocates the Halloween of old with the Halloween of today. Just because Halloween in its roots was Catholic does not mean that Halloween as it is celebrated today is Catholic. Halloween has become undeniably mixed up with evil practices and imagery. It’s virtually impossible to celebrate Halloween without exposing (and potentially desensitizing) ourselves to this imagery. Unlike Christmas, Halloween’s secular turn was not innocent; it was dark. Families are right to be cautious about a holiday that presents death and gore as fun and innocent. To say that the secular version of Halloween is worthy of our participation simply because some aspects of it used to be Christian is a weak argument. 

Additionally, the historical argument diminishes the fact that Halloween practices don’t come from exclusively Christian traditions. They also come from pagan ones. For example, the practice of trick-or-treating does not only come from the Christian tradition of souling. It also has roots in the Celtic pagan feast of Samhain, on which people would dress in disguises so evil spirits couldn’t bother them, and the Scottish and Irish tradition of “guising,” dressing up in costumes and performing small tricks in exchange for food or coins. Scottish and Irish immigrants brought all of these traditions overseas with them—the pagan as well as the Christian—and they all influenced what we call trick-or-treating today. Tracing the practices of Halloween back to exclusively Christian roots is not as straightforward as some would like to believe. 

But the argument from modernity also has issues. Those who believe that Halloween belongs exclusively to the devil are perhaps giving up the fight too soon. If Halloween was originally All Hallows’ Eve, an important day on the Christian liturgical calendar, then why surrender it to the forces of evil? An attack from Satan is not a reason to step out of the arena. It is a reason to step in and fight the good fight, bringing light to the darkness and combating evil with good. If Satan’s army works harder on Halloween, then Christians should too. We have a duty on Halloween night, and it is not to simply lock our doors and be passive.

So what are Catholics to do? In the end, the answer is not as simple as either side would like it to be. To start, we must admit that the world’s version of Halloween is not trying to glorify God. Most people aren’t trying to remember their mortality and cling to the things of heaven when they put witches, skeletons, and dismembered body parts in their lawns. Evil is at work on this night, and it would be foolish to turn a blind eye to this. As Christians we must be cognizant and prudent about the desensitization that happens when we expose ourselves to darkness. If we pretend that there is a “fun” or “innocent” version of darkness, we are playing right into the enemy’s hands. 

However, we also ought not give up the fight. Catholics can and should reclaim Halloween, just not in the way that some think. Catholics won’t reclaim Halloween simply by going to secular Halloween parties or trick-or-treating. Catholics won’t reclaim Halloween by participating in haunted houses or watching horror movies. Catholics never reclaimed anything in the world by simply doing what everyone else was already doing. 

Catholics will reclaim Halloween by going to Mass on the evening of October 31. Catholics will reclaim Halloween by praying for their departed family members by name on that night. They will reclaim Halloween by inviting their friends to a Rosary walk at the local cemetery. Above all, Catholics will reclaim Halloween by honoring its place within the larger celebration of Hallowtide, and especially by leaning into the culmination of the feast two days later on All Saints’ Day, when we celebrate the Church triumphant over death in all her glory.
